quote: Giebt es eine wohl definirte [-Frage-], auf die sinnlichen Dinge bezügliche Frage, welche eine Antwort haben muss und die gleichwohl sich nicht beantworten lässt.
english: Is there a well-defined question, relating to sensible things, which must have an answer and which nevertheless cannot be answered?
topic: Philosophical questions on whether human reason can answer every question it poses itself (decidability, squaring the circle, contradictory results), followed by a Plücker-type formula for the dimension of plane algebraic curves.

triage.modern_statement: This is a philosophical and foundational question, not a precise theorem. Hilbert asks whether there is a well-posed question that must have a definite answer, yet cannot be answered by any finite chain of reasoning. In modern terms it can be read two ways. (a) Within mathematics: is there a well-defined statement that is true or false but cannot be proved or disproved from a given axiom system? Equivalently, is there a well-defined problem that no algorithm can decide? (b) The broader reading, suggested by the phrase 'relating to sensible things', is about empirical knowledge: Du Bois-Reymond's 'ignorabimus' thesis that some questions about the natural world can never be answered. Hilbert's answer was 'no'. He later called this the 'axiom of solvability' of every mathematical problem (Paris 1900) and summed it up in 1930 as 'Wir müssen wissen, wir werden wissen.'
triage.answered_by: Hilbert's question has no single paper that settles it. The best-known later answer to the mathematical reading is Gödel's incompleteness theorems (1931). The other is the negative solution of the Entscheidungsproblem (decision problem) by Church and Turing (1936). The secondary literature says these results falsified Hilbert's conviction, at least in its formal, axiom-relative version. I did not manage to retrieve a separate source for Church and Turing, so that part rests on standard history. The empirical reading about 'sensible things' is still a philosophical matter and has no mathematical resolution.

evidence.claim: A Journal of Humanistic Mathematics article discusses Hilbert's 'axiom of solvability': his conviction that every mathematical problem can be solved in a finite number of steps. It says the question of solvability is commonly identified with the decision problem. It also says this conviction was falsified by Gödel's proof and by the negative results for the decision problem.

In the 1900 Paris lecture, Hilbert called the solvability of every mathematical problem an axiom. He asked whether it is peculiar to mathematics or 'possibly a general law' of thought. Feferman's paper discusses this.

Hilbert repeated his rejection of 'ignoramus et ignorabimus' in his address of 8 September 1930 to the Society of German Scientists and Physicians. This connects the diary question to Du Bois-Reymond's ignorabimus debate about the limits of natural science.
Oxford lecture notes on Hilbert's Programme and Gödel's incompleteness theorems quote Hilbert's 1900 conviction of the solvability of every mathematical problem as the backdrop to Gödel's results.

triage.why: The diary entry is Hilbert's early, private version of his 'non-ignorabimus' conviction. He published it publicly in the introduction to the 1900 Paris problems lecture, not as one of the 23 numbered problems, and again in the 1930 Königsberg address. For mathematics, the question was answered in the negative relative to formal systems by Gödel (1931) and the undecidability results of Church and Turing (1936); the secondary sources found say this explicitly. However, the note speaks of questions 'relating to sensible things', which points to the empirical or physical version of the debate, and that has no definitive answer. Undecidability and independence results remain active research areas, for example independence in set theory and undecidability in physics, but the note is too informal to tie to one specific theorem. That is why confidence is medium rather than high.
